stages.sub: Why competition rules can stop firms growing the way they want to.

steps.q: Two big supermarket chains want to merge and together would control 70% of the market. Would every customer welcome this, or might someone object?
steps.right: Someone, such as a watchdog, might object
steps.hint: Think about who checks whether a merger harms customers, not just the two firms involved.

steps.q: That merged supermarket now controls 70% of sales, with no rival close behind. Can smaller rivals easily compete with it on price or choice?
steps.right: No, it would be very hard for them
steps.wrong: Yes, just as easily as before
steps.hint: With one firm holding most of the market, how much power do the others have left?

steps.q: A government body reviews mergers like this and has the power to block them or force a firm to sell off parts of its business. Why would such a body exist?
steps.right: To stop firms dominating markets and harming consumers
steps.wrong: To help the biggest firms merge faster
steps.hint: Whose interest is being protected when mergers and dominant firms are reviewed?

steps.q: A firm wants to grow by merging with a rival, but knows the watchdog may block it or force changes. Does this rule make growing by merger easier or harder?
steps.right: Harder, growth can be limited or blocked
steps.wrong: Easier, the rules guide firms through mergers
steps.hint: If a plan can be blocked before it happens, what does that do to a firm's ability to grow that way?
